en: Now, he explains the drawing of the lines for the maṇḍala common to all maṇḍalas:
"One part [is] thin; at the end of the third, there are seven [parts] in the fourth."
One should draw each part as slender as a slender portion.
One part and seven small parts; at the end of the third, for the fourth, draw one small part, one small part, and one small part, making them equal.
The thread extends to the tip of the awn; from there follows the circle of filaments.
The lotus garland is two mātrās, and the banner garland is also two mātrās.
Reaching the very tip of its own apex, from there [proceed] a circular golden line, two units of the lotus garland, and two units of the vajra garland.
The garland of rays consists of four measures; one should fashion everything according to the meter.
Thus, by means of the grid, the thread is established in accordance with all mandalas.
The four small parts of the garland of light rays should all be made circular; thus, the lines drawn in that manner extend correctly across the entire mandala.
Due to the distinction of deities, the drawing of the lines differs slightly within the mandala of the root [deity] according to the Buddhas; however, no such difference exists on the exterior.
With slight distinctions regarding the deities, within the fundamental maṇḍala, the wise one should perceive the distinctions of the lines and their inseparability on the outside.
Now the elision of the *dvārādi* group is stated in due order:
seven above, two across, two above and across, and two across and above.
Now, the classification of the gates and so forth shall be explained according to their sequence: there are seven above, two on each side, and two above and on two sides.
One should erase three [units] above, three on the *polī*, four above that again,
six from the altar (*vedī*), and likewise three each on the cloth and the pillar.
Above, three by three are empty; likewise, four are again above. Six are likewise removed from the pedestal; there are three by three for the cloth and the pillar.
One should erase four lines at the gateway of Brahmā, two on each of the two sides, and likewise erase them at the edge of the cloth; the gems are situated in the middle of the half-necklace.

In the Brahmā [mandala], two squares are removed from each of the four corners; likewise, they are removed at the edge of the cloth. In the center, there is a jeweled lattice (*ratnajāla*) with half-lattices.
Likewise, on the *bakulī* and the *kramaśīrṣa*, as well as on the ground of the *rajovedī*,
one should erase the lower lines of all the sūtras up to the corner.
One should completely erase all the lines that exceed the corners—namely, those of the eastern section, the arrow-head section, the painted area, and the platform site.
By this it is said:
"The door is considered to be one-eighth of the wheel, and is held to be without a pedestal."
The turrets and the deity-bands are equal in measure to the doors.
The gates are one-eighth of the wheel; they are held to be free from pedestals. Each gate-arch is equal in measure to the gate itself, and likewise is the divine panel.

The altar (vedī) extends halfway across the doors on all sides; likewise, there are the cheeks (kapola), the side-wings (pakṣaka), the pearl necklace (hāra), the half-necklace (ardhahāra), the moon, the sun, the ribbon-band (paṭṭa), the garland-festoon (sragdāma), and the fillet-band (paṭṭikā).
The ground for the dust is half of that, outside of the grounds for the root-line and the sūtra-line.

The entire platform has half-gates on all sides; likewise, it has [ornaments] on its edges and faces, as well as lattices, half-lattices, suns, moons, and cloths of flower garlands. Half of that is the area for colors, which lies outside the line of the base. This is what is explained.
The deity-strip, however,
is within the root-line.
The altar, however, is called both the *dhāraṇī-paṭṭī* (retaining-cloth) and the *nartana-paṭṭī* (dancing-cloth).
Regarding the altar, it is also referred to as the "cloth of dhāraṇīs" and the "intermediate cloth."
The venerable Ārya Nāgabuddhipāda, however, does not accept the *añcalapaṭṭī*, the *antarālapaṭṭī*, or the *skandhapaṭṭī*. For he says:
"The door shall consist of one-eighth of the [mandala] circle, and likewise the decorative bands for the deities (*devatāpaṭṭikā*)."

"The turret (niryūha), the cheek (kapola), and the side-panel (pakṣaka) are equal in measure to the door. Thus say the scriptures. This is according to the scriptural authority which states: "The turret is one-eighth of the door; the divine cloth (devapaṭṭa) is likewise. The architrave (toraṇa) is the same measure as the door; the corner and the side are also thus."
Here, the ground situated between the two door-arches (dvāratoraṇa) is called the *antarālapaṭṭī*, the *andhakārapaṭṭī*, and the *pellīpaṭṭī*. || 0 ||
Here, in the middle space between the gates and the archways, there is what is called the "intermediate cloth," the "cloth of darkness," and also the "void."
The archway (toraṇa) is three times the size of the door, and it consists of eleven tiers (paṭṭikā).
The *āmra*, *bakula*, jewel, and pillar (*dhurā*) each occupy four units (*kṛśa*).
The archway is threefold compared to the door; it likewise has eleven tiers. The *āmra*, *bakula*, jewel, and pillar each consist of four small units (*kṛśa*).
One and a half *kṛśa* for the *andhārī*, one *kṛśa* for the *varaṇḍaka*;
likewise again for the *andhārī*, the *bakulī*, and the *maṇi*.
One and a half *kṛśas* for the *andhārī*, one *kṛśa* for the *varaṇḍaka*; likewise again for the *andhārī*, the *bakulī*, and the *maṇi*.

The *khura* measures should each be one *mātrā*, and the *kramaśīrṣa* likewise by measure. Having declared their measurement vertically, it is now described horizontally: the *rmig pa* shall be one small part (*cha chung*) each, and the *mnga' yab* shall be the same. These have been explained according to their vertical dimensions; now their width shall also be stated.
The sixteenfold measure would be the Āmāra, while the Bakulī is recorded as eighteen.
The jeweled hooves should likewise be made; Andhāra shall be fourteen [finger-widths].
The *bre-phul* shall be sixteen, and for the eastern bud it is said to be eighteen. The jeweled hooves should likewise be made; Andhāra shall be fourteen.
The varaṇḍa should be sixteen [units] and the andhārikā twelve again.
There are fourteen *bakulī* [fingers] on the two ruby hooves;
likewise, there are sixteen on the copper [hooves], and again twelve on the dark [hooves]; there are fourteen on the front hoof, and the same for the jewel hoof.
There may be ten spokes for the *kramaśīrṣa* [wheel], and the *dharmacakra* shall have two *mātrās*;
the *śūka* shall likewise have two *mātrās*. This is consistent with all mandalas.
The shaft of the arrow becomes ten [units], while the wheel of Dharma consists of two small units; the rim likewise consists of two small units—all of these pervade the entire mandala.
Having held the thread with three and a half measures (mātrās), one should fashion the Brahma-line;
that circle, measuring seven mātrās, is for the sake of the face and is most beautiful.
Having fixed the Brahma-line with a cord of three and a half small units, one should beautifully mark a circle there with a cord of seven small units for the sake of the curvature.
Again, at a distance of three *mātrās* to the right and left of the *brahman*,
one should likewise rotate a circle, beautiful like a half-moon.
To the right and left of Brahmā, once again, within a distance of three minor units, one should likewise draw a circle; it should be made beautiful like a half-moon.
Within that very [circle], at a distance of half a mātrā,
the wise one should likewise rotate [the instrument] again for the purpose of drawing the jewels and so forth.

Within that very [space], a circle should again be drawn up to half a minor unit (kala) for the purpose of drawing the jewels and so forth; thus it should be circumscribed by one of noble intelligence.
One should erase all the lower lines from every side in the center;
then, a second thread should be applied vertically along the borders.
One should completely remove all internal excesses; one should apply the lines above and below the woolen cloths according to the second [method].
Indeed, for the sake of beauty, having carefully placed that [mark] even within the circle,
one should again place it within the four-finger-breadth of Brahmā, at the end of the three doors.
Striving for the sake of beauty, even within that which is crooked, one should grasp a quarter-part of Brahmā and again [place it] between the three gates.
For the sake of the boundary, one should rotate a beautiful thread like a half-moon;
and at a distance of three *mātrās* to its right and left as well.
For the sake of the corners, draw a beautiful line curved like a half-moon; likewise, on both the right and left sides, [extend it] for a distance of three small units.
In that very manner, the wise Vajrācārya should rotate the circle;
its spokes emerge from the mouths of sea-monsters and are adorned with garlands of flames.
The wise Vajra Master should draw a circle in the manner of suchness; it should be adorned with a flaming garland and a horn emerging from the mouth of a makara.
Above the archway, a wheel should be drawn, with a male and female deer on its two sides;
their horns should point upward and extend slightly beyond the half-mātrā [of the arch].
On the surface of the wheel above the archway, one should draw a male and female deer at a distance of half a *kala* [unit of measure], with their necks held upright.
Two beautiful parasols should be drawn at their tails,
along with a canopy beneath the archway, provided with bells and chowries.
At their tails, two beautiful parasols should be painted; beneath the archway, there should be a canopy equipped with bells and a fly-whisk.
A perfected vidyādhara couple, or else two ḍākinīs,
enter the maṇḍala again, their hands busy with the substances for worship.
Alternatively, the accomplished vidyādhara or the ḍākinī herself as the essence—those who hold the offering substances in their hands—should enter the maṇḍala once again.
Swans, peacocks, kiṃnarīs, lions,
and other such beautiful creatures should be painted on the two edges of the banners, as well as small decorative flags.
Peacocks, garuḍas, humans, or lions and other such magnificent birds should be painted at the ends of the woolen cloths; likewise, small banners [should be depicted].
On the right and left of the Āra, there are wish-fulfilling trees standing in water-jars,
endowed with the eight jewels and adorned all around with creepers.

On both the right and left sides of all [the vases], there are wish-fulfilling trees situated within the vases; they are endowed with the eight precious gems and are completely filled with creeping vines.
They are surrounded on all sides by every kind of flower and fruit, by the warbling of various birds, and by *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, and others.
It was completely surrounded on all sides by various flowers and fruits, by all the birds uttering their diverse songs, and by those who have attained the vidyādharas.
All of them should be depicted with forms emerging from clouds;
banners should be placed at the doors, situated upon jars on the left and right sides.
One should draw all those forms clearly situated within the clouds; at the gates, one should place victory banners, and to the right and left of the vase, [one should place them].
Marked with lions, swans, peacocks, crocodiles, and fish,
their quarters resounded with bells and fluttering, variegated banners.
It is marked with lions, elephants, peacocks, crocodiles, and fish; it possesses various fluttering banners and resounds with the tinkling of bells.
In the corners, umbrellas should be made, as well as other small banners;
they should be free from [excessive] marks and the like, and be of various colors on all sides.
One should fashion parasols for the shrines, as well as small banners; these should be free from [worldly] marks and the like, and made entirely of various colors.
Moreover,
there is a further distinction regarding those who dwell in charnel grounds within the mandala.
The garland of light rays (*raśmimālā*) is two units (*mātrā*), and the vajra-garland (*vajrāvalī*) is one unit;
the lotus-garland (*padmāvalī*) should be made likewise, and the charnel ground (*śmaśāna*) is four units.
Writing, however, should be performed with diligence when meeting those who are worthy;
it must never be done by one who guards the samaya when encountering those who are unworthy.
When those who are fortunate have arrived, one should write with great diligence; when those who lack fortune have arrived, one should not do it at all, even if it means violating the samaya.
Thus it is said in the *Vajraḍākatantra*:
"Outside, the halo of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) is twice the measure of the dust-ground (*rajobhūmi*)."
For it is stated: "But outside the Cakravāḍa [mountain range] are the eight cremation grounds, beginning with Vṛkṣa."

This is also taught in the *Vajraḍāka-tantra*: "Twice the measure of the colored ground is the outer mandala of light; outside of that circumambulatory area are the eight charnel grounds, such as the trees and so forth. Thus it is said.
Moreover, Ānandagarbha has further described the archway (*toraṇa*):

the King (16), the three-fold fault (18, 18, 18), the Sun (12), the King (16), the direction (10), and the three-fold Manu (14, 14, 14), and the directions (10)— this sequence of *mātrikās* across the bands of the archway is also consistent.

Furthermore, the archway of Ānandagarbha shall also be described: "The three faults of man, the sun, the directions of man, and the three [of man]; the directions, the straight line, and the minor parts—these constitute the successive tiers of the archway. This too is the "universal liberation."

Furthermore, in that case where the door is one-tenth of the wheel or one-ninth of the wheel, and the mandala, extending up to the *kramaśīrṣa*, measures sixty-four *mātrās*, in that case the archway (*toraṇa*) shall be twelve *mātrās* in width and four *mātrās* in height; however, it shall consist of eleven bands (*paṭṭikā*).

Furthermore, in whichever direction the courtyard becomes one-tenth or nine-ninths of the wheel, there will be sixty-four small units (kalā) up to the end of the makara-torana on the mandala; in that direction, the width of the archway (toraṇa) will be twelve small units and its height four small units. However, the cloth (paṭa) shall be eleven [small units].
And so it is said:
||| Thus also: |||
Bakulī, Ratnā, Sthānā, Svarṇā, Makarā, Kāñcanā, Sthānā, Ratnā, Saṃsthānā, Svarṇā, and Kramaśīrṣakā— these are [the types of] that.
Śarbu, Rinchen, Nasa, and Ser; Chu-srin, then Ser and Nasa; Rinchen, Yangdag-nasa, Ser, and Da-yab—these are they.
"Sthāna" is a synonym for "hoof.
"Gnas" is a synonym for "hoof."
The measurement from the top should be understood according to the divisions of the *mahābhāga* parts:
eight (*vasu*), eight (*vasu*), twelve (*sūrya*), twenty-four (*jina*), eight (*vasu*), and twenty-four (*jina*);
twelve (*ravi*), eight (*vasu*), twelve (*sūrya*), twelve (*jina*), and eight (*vasu*) in sequence.

By means of the divisions of *cha* and *chen*, they are called the measurements of height: *nor*, *nor*, *nyi ma*, *rgyal ba*, *nor*, *rgyal ba*, *nyi ma*, *nor*, *nyi ma*, and *rgyal ba nor*, respectively.
Having described the measurement vertically, their horizontal measurement is now stated:
from the right and left of Brahmā, at an interval of one and a half *mātrās*,
there is a fillet (*paṭṭī*) of one and a half *mātrās* and a thread (*sūtra*) of two *mātrās*.
The second and third [syllables] are two mātrās each from the four-mātrā [unit];
from the four-mātrā [unit], the fourth is two mātrās; from three and a half [units], the *iṣu* (the fifth) is three and a half;
from three, the sixth is three mātrās, and after that, there are three [more].
Eight measures, seven measures, one, and six measures for the last;
outside that, at the end of the Veda-measures, a circle from two measures, and likewise [another] from two measures;
a line from two measures, a circle from four measures, and then the final [circle].

This has been explained as the measurement for the height; now the width of these shall be described. On the right and left of Brahmā, at the edge of the ocean, one and a half *kalās* [from the center] is the second line. Likewise, from two *kalās*, the second and third [sections] are two *kalās* and four *kalās* respectively; and the fourth is four *kalās*.

Two small units (kalā), and from the half [unit] the third is two and a half; from the third, the sixth is three small units; from there, the eighth small unit occurs three times; the seventh is one, and at the end is the sixth. Therefore, at the end of the small units of the Vedas, the circle is two small units; likewise, the line of the circle with two small units is at the end of the fourth small unit.
Thus, we have described both positions: that there are three-fold arches (toraṇa) at the side-doors for animals, and also [the other position].
Thus, in terms of the width, it is also three times the size of the gate and its archway. In this way, I have described both dimensions.

Regarding the second position, it is stated that the outer maṇḍala is twice the size of the central maṇḍala; this extends up to the circular line of the lotus filaments, prior to the [central] thread.
According to the first position, however, it extends from the central maṇḍala together with its retinue up to the garland of light rays.
As for the first position, it is as far as the garland of light rays from the central maṇḍala together with its retinue.

The claim that "the architrave (toraṇa) is fourteen mātrās beyond the pillar of the architrave and within the circular line of the lotus filaments" is rejected, as it is inconsistent with both positions. The assertion that "the architrave is four units (mātrā) on this side of the circular line of the lotus filaments, beyond the pillar of the architrave" is also discarded, as it does not accord with either of the two systems.

Here, at the junction of the door and the *niryūha*, one should draw upon the *mātrikā* a gem situated on a crescent moon, which is red, yellow, dark green, or black, marked above with either a half-vajra or a complete vajra. It is as follows:

Here, at the junction of the doors and the door-arches, on a space of one small unit (*cha chung*), one should draw a red, yellow, green, or black jewel resting upon the lunar crescent, marked above either by a half-vajra or a complete vajra. Thus it is said:
Outside the ground of dust, at the junctions of the corners, gates, and turrets,
it is illuminated on all sides by sprouts of vajras, jewels, and moons.
According to this statement, the pillars of the archways are situated within jars placed upon a square altar.

For it is said: "On the outer corners of the site of the colors, at the junctions of the doors and door-arches, there are full moons marked with jewels and vajras, blazing intensely on all sides. The pillars of the archways rest upon vases situated on square pedestals.
And likewise:
the archway is threefold from the door; the rafters extend from the mouths of sea-monsters;
the pillars of the archway rise up, emerging from the base-pots of the altar-platform.

Thus it is said. At their base and summit is a jeweled band (*maṇibandha*), and in the middle, upon an elephant, stands a lion with its trunk raised. From the profusion of jeweled leaf-patterns hanging from the arches (*toraṇa*), there hang, as is aesthetically appropriate, colorful streamers of cloth—red, yellow, and so forth—or variegated ones, as well as fly-whisks (*cāmara*) with jeweled handles.

Furthermore, it is said: "From the makara’s mouth to the bull, [the distance] is three times that from the archway to the gate; the pillar of the archway situated above the pedestal and vase is firmly established. Their bases and tips are adorned with jewels. In the center, upon an elephant, is a lion supported by its haunches.
From the rafters of the archways hang jeweled pendants that spread out, beautifully draped in colors such as red and yellow, or various cloths and jeweled tassels attached to fly-whisks.

However, some say that on the border-strip (*añcalapaṭṭikā*) there is a lion upon an elephant with a necklace hanging from its mouth; but in the middle of the pillar there is simply a mirror. On the jewel-strip (*ratnapaṭṭī*), however, there are triangular, square, oblong, and circular *tilakas* in sequence, and jewel-knots (*ratnabandha*) on each side of every single pillar.

In some cases, it is said that upon the silken cloth of the canopy, there are necklaces hanging from the mouths of lions atop elephants, and mirrors in the center of the pillars. As for the jeweled cloths, on their edges there are triangles, squares, bindus, and circles, which are sequentially inlaid with jewels at the sides of each pillar.

Upon the fillet of the necklaces and half-necklaces, outside the four golden girdles, there are pearl necklaces strung with red thread, disgorged from the mouths of sea-monsters (*makara*). On both sides, above and below, are half-necklaces with rubies set in gold at their centers; on the sides of these necklaces hang streams of jewel-garlands slightly shorter in length, and there are half-necklaces beautiful at their tips with large gems set in gold. Furthermore, fly-whisks with jeweled handles and bells, as well as fly-whisks, hang down in some places.

On the cloth with lattice and half-lattice patterns, on the outer surface of the golden waistband, there was a pearl necklace emerging from the mouth of a makara, strung on red thread, with gold-inlaid jewels at both ends, above, and below, situated in the center.

On both sides of the two faces, there are hanging strings of jewels that lean slightly outward; they possess thick, beautiful gems bound with gold at their tips and are adorned with half-lattices. In some places, there are jeweled-handled fly-whisks and bells, with fly-whisks hanging from their edges.
However, some say that on both sides of the half-necklace (ardhahāra) hang beautiful flower-garland half-nets, and at their sides are half-nets of variegated cloth.
Some say that on both sides of the half-necklace hang beautiful flower-garland half-nets, and on those sides are half-nets of various garments.
Others [adorned] the corners with half-necklaces of lovely flower garlands and necklaces of fine silk ribbons.
In some cases, within the interior of a necklace, there is a solar mandala marked by a lotus, a crescent moon, and a half-vajra; in some cases, a jewel;
and in some cases, a vajra resting upon a lotus.
Thus, this sequence for laying out the lines and drawing outside the root mandala is common to all mandalas.
Such is the sequence for drawing the lines and painting [the mandala] outside the root maṇḍala; it is common to all maṇḍalas.
Now, however, the specific distinction regarding the interior must be stated.
Now, the internal distinctions shall be explained:
from the *brahmā* meter consisting of eight morae (*mātrā*) in the previously introduced sūtras,
one *vṛtta* is to be given, and again at the end, one consisting of eight morae.

Having carefully extended the previous lines, one should draw a circle starting from the Brahma-line at the point of the "Sage" (the third minor unit); then, [another circle] should be drawn at the end of the "Wealth" (the eighth minor unit).
There, a vajra-garland should be made, and the garland of light rays consists of one *mātrā*.
Again, on the right and left of Brahmā, at intervals of two *mātrās* each:

*tatra vajrāvalī kāryā raśmimālā tu mātrikā | brahmaṇo dakṣiṇe vāme dvidvimātrāntare punaḥ ||* A vajra-garland should be fashioned there, while the circle of light rays is of one measure (*mātrikā*). Furthermore, on the right and left of Brahmā, at intervals of two measures (*mātrā*) each.
One should preserve the pillar-base slab (stambhapattī) of the matrix (mātrikā), but the others should be erased;
within the interior, there are nine square cells in the cardinal directions.
Having properly protected each small square of the cloth, one removes the others; the essence of the squares is the four corners, and those very directions are [the basis].
And in the intermediate directions, there are triangles for Locanā and the others; furthermore,
on the deity frieze, they are located on the grounds of Rūpavajrā and the rest.
One should erase all the lower lines on every side;
in this manner, the mandala of Mañjuvajra will be formed according to the sequence.
Whatever residual hopes there may be, all of them are completely eradicated; through such a sequence, one becomes the maṇḍala of Mañjuvajra.
This same procedure applies even when the central deity is placed within [the maṇḍala]. By this, the lines for arranging the principal deity elsewhere are also established.
By this [method], [one draws] a square with four doors, adorned with four arches (toraṇas).
One should mark out the outer maṇḍala, joined with four lines;
it is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, and provided with four lines in equal proportion. Thus the outer maṇḍala should be marked.
Within that, there is a wheel resembling an eight-maṇḍala;
it is circular on all sides,
with a radius equal to half of the outer wheel.
It is auspicious, fashioned with wheel-pillars and the like, and encircled by a garland of vajras.
It is stated that the ground for the lines of the wheel-pillars and so forth is equal to the ground for the colored powders.

It is also explained that: "Adorned with pillars of the wheel and so forth, and beautified by a surrounding vajra garland, the ground of the lines for the pillars of the wheel and so forth is equal to the ground for the colored powders."
This very same method of drawing the lines applies even to the maṇḍala taught in the *Piṇḍīkrama*. However, the specific details are stated once more:
This very same method of drawing the lines applies even to the maṇḍala taught in the *Piṇḍīkrama*. However, the specific details are stated once more:

Having drawn two circles within the center, one should place eight pillars between the Brahma-line and the corner-lines at intervals of one unit (mātrā) using the diagonal lines. *garbhe vṛttadvayaṃ dattvā brahmakoṇakasūtrayoḥ | madhye tu mātrayā stambhā aṣṭau syuḥ khaṇḍasūtrakaiḥ ||* Having given two circles in the center, there shall be eight pillars between the Brahma-line and the corner-lines, each measuring one unit, by means of the diagonal lines.
There are three lines in the cardinal and intermediate directions within the central mass;

likewise, there are lines in the center of the two circles which serve as the support for Rūpavajrā and the others, and specifically on the bands of the Ratna family, there are lines for the Bodhisattvas.

"In the cardinal and intermediate directions are triangles; in the two central circles as well, one removes the *rekhas* situated within and the *rekhas* situated in the squares of Rūpavajrā and the others, who abide in the jewel-like bodhicitta."
In the *Śrīsampuṭodbhava-tantra*, regarding the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva,

within the wheel consisting of thirty-seven [deities], on the right and left sides of Brahmā: As taught in the *Śrīsampuṭa-tantra*, in the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva, which consists of thirty-seven [deities] in its wheel, [it is located] on the right and left sides of Brahmā.
Having omitted an interval of one and a half *mātrās*, there is a double-thread (*dvisūtra*) consisting of half a *mātrā*;
having omitted a three-*mātrā* verse, the *vajrāvalī* consists of half a *mātrā*.
Henceforth, having discarded half a *kalā* from the center, two lines for the half-*kalā* should be drawn; discarding three *kalās*, there is a circle, and at the half-*kalā* is a vajra-garland.
The garland of rays shall consist of half-mātrās; then there is an interval of three mātrās.
Within that interval of half-mātrās is a circle, and in its center is a row of lotuses.
On one side, there shall be a garland of light rays; from within three small units, returning again to half a small unit, in the center of that circle, there shall also be a garland of lotuses.
Again, there is a meter of three morae; again, with an interval of half a mora;
again, the garland of wheels in their midst, and the supreme ground consists of three morae.
From three small units (aṃśas) it becomes circular; again, at half a small unit from that, there is a garland of wheels in its center. On the other ground, there are three small units.
In the auspicious mandala of the Śrījñānaḍākinīs, which consists of thirteen [deities],
the thread should be three mātras from the Brahma-thread, while the other two threads should be one mātra each.
The glorious thirteen-fold mandala of the Wisdom Ḍākinī is beautiful in its essential nature. From the Brahma-thread, two lines are formed from three parts of a *mātrikā*.
Again, having abandoned six measures, one should compose a single metrical line;
and again, a metrical line consisting of measures for the purpose of the Vajrāvalī.
Again, having discarded six parts, one should draw a single circle. Furthermore, upon that circular [area], there is the mark of a vajra-garland.
Furthermore, for the sake of the garland of rays, from another matrix, there is again the supreme ground of four measures; one should erase the lower lines. ||o||
For the sake of the *raśmimālā*, one should again remove a small portion from another; on the ground of the other, four small portions and an additional fraction should be subtracted.
The mandala of the fourfold Hevajrarāja consisting of seventeen deities,
as well as that of the fourfold Vajrāmṛta, and those of the goddess Nairātmyā and Kurukullā;
To those who possess the nature of the seventeen [deities], to the four kings of Hevajra, to the four vajra-nectars, and to the immeasurable Kuru-kulle maṇḍalas—
Outside the Brahma-line, four circles should be drawn with four lines;
they are one-eighth of a *mātrā* in thickness, and their distance from each other is two and a half *mātrās*.
Outside from the Brahma-line, one should draw four circular lines; [the first] at three and a half units, the second at eight units, and the final one at two and a half units.
The first [part] is five and a quarter *mātrās*, the second for the petals is two [mātrās],
and the third for the vajra-garland is one and eight-sixteenths of a *mātrā*.
In five parts including the leg, the second and third [parts] are for the petals; the vajra-garland is eight parts including a fraction.
The fourth [square] of Raśmi consists of four measures (mātrikā), while the remaining [squares] are the earth consisting of six measures.
One should erase the Brahma-thread and the diagonal thread from the center. ||o||
The fourth is the small portion of the garland of light; the remaining grounds are six small portions. Within, the Brahma-lines and the corner-lines are to be erased.
Of this fourfold maṇḍala of the body of Hevajra, which consists of nine [deities],
having excluded Brahmā, the circle [of the central deity] is five *mātrās*;
the other [circles] are of double that measure.
Outside of that is a square grid marked by a garland of vajras;
some say that there itself is a row of pots—thus says the knower of mantras.
"Outside of that, the circular portion is marked with a vajra garland; on that very [portion] is a garland of vases. Thus it is said. Some practitioners of mantra-vidyā speak in this way.
The mandala of the form of Buddhakapāla and that called Mahāmāyā is said to be equal to that; its measurement is not exceeded by even the slightest degree.
The body of Buddhakapāla and that which is called Mahāmāyā—these are taught as the mandala of equality; in this measure, there is neither excess nor deficiency.
The marking with lines in the maṇḍala of the Lord Vajra-hūṃkāra is fixed:
having set aside two and a half mātrās on both sides of the two Brahma-lines.

Regarding the definitive marking of the lines for the maṇḍala of the Protector Vajra-hūṃkāra: having set aside two and a half small units from both sides of the Brahma-line, [the center is established].

The center of the filaments should be circular, and the petals should be five morae in measure; then, leaving aside one mora, [the design should be extended] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

The circle of Ge-sar becomes [complete] from five small units (kala) up to the petals; then, having completely discarded those small units, [it is established] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
There are seven and a half measures for the eight lotuses;
indeed, one should make a three-measure lotus at the eastern and western gates.
It also becomes eight lotuses, each measuring seven and a half small units (*aṃśa*). At the eastern and western gates, one should make lotuses measuring three small units.
The method of laying out the lines for the Cakrasaṃvara-Vārāhī maṇḍala is as follows:
from the base, half [the width], then one and a half, then half, then one and a half, and then half again.
Just as for the maṇḍala lines of Cakrasaṃvara and Vārāhī, from the channel-lines [the measurements are] half, half, and four; half, half, and four, and a half.
Having rotated the circle of the Guru by two and a half *kaṇapādas* (one and a quarter *adhyuṣṭhas*),
one should then lay down the lines for the purpose of the enclosure (*ārā*).
At three and a half [units], four parts, and from three and a half petals, one should draw the circles of the gurus there; then, having struck the lines for the purpose of the spokes.
Having left an interval of one and a half mātrās to the right and left of Brahmā, the thread should be laid out, reaching as far as the two root-threads.
To the right and left of Brahmā, having set aside a space of one and a half minor units (kala), one should carefully apply the lines up to the central lines.
Having left a space of half a measure, the mantra-practitioner should likewise stretch the thread again;
he should likewise lay down four threads at the corners.
Having left a space of half a small finger-breadth, one should again strike the lines in that same manner; likewise for the corners, the mantrin should apply four lines.
The Sūtra issued from Brahmā extends up to the two supreme Mātrās;
then, having emerged again from that, it enters back into that very same place in like manner.
The thread definitely emerges from the Brahma-hole; as far as the limit of two *mātrās*, it emerges again from there and enters back into that very same [hole].
Having emerged even from that, the thread [reaches] once more up to the limit of two *mātrās*;
then, having issued forth from that, it enters back into that thread.
Then again,
it emerges from that until it reaches the limit of two *mātrās*;
then, having emerged once more from that, it enters back into that Brahman.
Again, having departed from that, it goes as far as two minor parts; then, departing once more from there, it enters into that Brahmā.
Just as it is on the right, so it is on the left, and likewise in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Within that too, there is a thread at an interval of half a mātrā.
Just as it is on the right, so it is on the left; likewise in the cardinal directions and the intermediate points, and likewise within that [area], up to half a minor unit.
By that same sequential method, one should fashion the beautiful *tilaka* and *maṇḍala* on the right and left sides, as they have emerged from the ocean of Saṃvara.
By means of the application of the stages of that very [reality], one should act upon what is neither right nor left; this arises from the ocean of Cakrasaṃvara, the maṇḍala of bindus and joy.
One should encircle the sides of the spokes with four extremely fierce vajras;
the remainder is an eight-petaled lotus, and its measurement should not exceed this by even the slightest bit.
On the surface of each spoke, it is surrounded by four extremely fierce vajras; the remainder consists of eight lotus petals, neither exceeding nor falling short of these proportions.

The garlands of Vajra, Padma, and Ari should be placed on the rims of the mind-wheel and the others; one should preserve the circular lines and the circular spokes, while the other [lines] may be omitted. Thus it is said. || 0 ||

On the rims of the wheels of the heart and so forth, there are garlands of vajras, lotuses, and wheels; they are encircled by circular lines and spokes. Having perfectly protected these, the others are removed.
The mandala of the Lord Buddhakapāla, who consists of twenty-five aspects, has been described as equal to that; however, its specific distinction shall now be stated.
To the Protector Buddhakapāla, who consists of twenty-five [deities], they proclaimed that maṇḍala; furthermore, there is a slight distinction.
Omitting the sixth metrical interval, one should provide a single, beautiful five-mora verse for the purpose of the petals, and another for the purpose of the filaments. ||o||

Having removed [the material] from within the sixth circle, one should provide a single circle measuring five small units at the edge of the petals; it is most beautiful for the purpose of the filaments.
Furthermore, within the wheel of Śrī Yogāmbara, having again left a space of three and a half mātrās from the interior of the base, one should cause a single circle to be made.
Within the mandala of the glorious Yogācāra space, one should also draw a single circle inside the lines of the channels, having set aside three and a half minor units.
Furthermore, there is the very beautiful *mātrika* meter of the *Vajrāvalī*;
then, having omitted one *trimātrika*, one should provide a single *vṛtta*.
Furthermore, upon the small circular portion, there is a most beautiful vajra garland. Then, having set aside three small portions, one circle should be bestowed.
Just as the laying out with the thread was described for the Piṇḍīkrama Maṇḍala,
so too is every other procedure for laying out the thread in this Maṇḍala exactly the same.
Just as the lines were explained for the mandala of the *Saṃpuṭa-krama*, so too are all the other lines in this mandala exactly the same.

Within the *mūlasūtra* is a second gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*) and a *ṭipi*; this is like the Mañjuvajra maṇḍala consisting of forty-three [deities] that will be described—this is one view. Another says: "The second gabled chamber is from the central gabled chamber. Yet another says: "There is no gabled chamber here, nor a vajra-fence as before. ||o||

Others maintain that within the central lines, there is a second celestial mansion (*vimāna*), which is like the maṇḍala of Mañjuvajra consisting of forty-three [deities], as will be explained. Some hold that the second celestial mansion is circular, distinct from the central celestial mansion. Others, however, say that there is no celestial mansion here at all.
"The vajra garland is as before. Thus it is said.
Of Yamāri, the King of Wrath, who consists of thirteen aspects,
there is a thread [marking] at the end of the seventh mātrā of Brahmā and at the end of the eighth.
Even for Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, who consists of thirteen [deities], one should apply the calculation up to seven parts less than Brahmā and also up to eight parts.
The diagonal lines should be drawn for the purpose of the vajra-garland;
in all directions, there are five-spoked vajras, each measuring eight units. ||o||
This concerns the peripheral lines. These are the marks of the vajra-garland; in each direction are five vajra-fences. This is the determination of the circular lines surrounding all parts.
In the mandala of the goddess Śrī Vajratārā, the marking with lines is fixed:
at the end of the three measures of Brahmā, there is a circle indicating the filaments.

Regarding the determination of the circumferential lines at three small units from the Brahma-line: at the end of three small units from the Brahma-line lies the circle of the tip of the central prong.
Outside of that, there is a circle of six measures serving as the basis for the row of petals.
Furthermore, one should remove the lines for the corners of Śaṃ (Śiva) and Brahmā. Thus it is said. ||o||
Therefore, it is surrounded by six minor parts; this is the mark of the garland of petals. One should erase the Brahmā-line situated there, as well as the diagonal lines.
Just as the marking out with threads is performed for the mandala of glorious Mañjuvajra, so too is it for the mandala of Mārīcī, who consists of twenty-five aspects. Oṃ.
Just as the lines for the mandala of glorious Mañjuvajra were drawn, so too are they for the twenty-five-fold mandala of the Radiant One (Marīcī).
Furthermore, in the thirteen-fold mandala of the Pañcarakṣā,
there should be a circle two mātras from the Brahma-line, indicating the location of the filaments.
The mandala of the five protections, which consists of thirteen [parts], is a circle at the tip of the pericarp, measuring two units from the Brahma-line.
Then, from four *mātrās*, one draws a very beautiful circle for the purpose of the petals;
then, at intervals of *mātrās* in the cardinal directions,
there are lotuses of eight *mātrās*.
The thread should be placed outside that [square], extending four units on all sides;
one should then remove the Brahma-thread as well as the corner-threads. ||o||
Outside of those lines, one should provide a square on all sides; likewise, the Brahma-lines and the diagonal lines should be erased again.
And within the mandala of the Vajradhātu, which consists of one hundred and fifty-three [units],
a thread measuring eight mātrās should be laid out inside the perimeter.
In the Vajradhātu maṇḍala as well, one should apply lines within the central area consisting of one hundred and fifty-three units, divided into eight minor parts.
In this way, however, there is the base of the second mandala,
provided with arches, turrets, and gates.
That itself is the second, the inner maṇḍala’s root lines; it is without a toraṇa arch, yet possesses door-surrounds and is symmetrical with the doors.
Immediately within the root [mandala], a circle should be drawn;
and again, a circle of one matra should be made for the purpose of the vajra-garland.
One should fashion a perfect circle reaching to the very end of the interior of the central channel; furthermore, upon that minor circle is the mark of a vajra.
Leaving an interval of two mātrās each to the right and left of Brahmā,
one should apply the thread up to the limit of the two circular threads.
On the right and left of Brahmā, having set aside a space of two *kalās* each, one should apply the lines between the two circular lines.
Furthermore, one should cause a thread to be placed at another interval for the purpose of marking;
thus, nine squares are formed through the omission of the Brahma-thread and the others. ||o||
From the center of the small squares, draw the lines once again; likewise, provide them for the purpose of the pillars. This results in nine compartments. Remove the Brahma-line and the others.
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, it is stated that the central peaked pavilion of the Trilokavijaya maṇḍala is equipped with archways. ||o||
The *Tattvasaṃgraha* states that for the maṇḍala of Trailokyavijaya, there is an inner celestial palace together with a gateway (*toraṇa*).
In the mandala of Mañjuvajra, which consists of forty-three [squares],
there should be a thread inside, at a distance of two doors from itself.
Within the mandala of Mañjuvajra, which consists of forty-three [deities], one should draw the lines inside the primary lines, up to a distance of two door-measures from oneself.
That [line] must be drawn by the mantra-practitioner up to the two corner-lines;
that very same [point] is the base of the second mandala within.
The mantra practitioner should also offer [the thread] between the two corner-lines; this very second [thread] is the fundamental line of the inner maṇḍala.
And likewise, one should cause a third mandala to be made, complete with arches, pilasters, and so forth, as well as its inner sanctum (garbha).
It should be provided with archways, doors, door-frames, and so forth; likewise, a third mandala should also be constructed within that one.
Just as there is a nine-compartment center within the Vajradhātu, so too should it be prepared here by the mantra-practitioner, well-encircled by a vajra-garland. ||o||
Just as within the Vajradhātu, so too here there shall be nine squares; this should be performed by the mantra-practitioners, well-encircled by a vajra-garland.
One should understand the laying out of the lines for the wheel of Vāgīśvara on the exterior to be equal to that of all other wheels; however, the specific details are stated again.
Regarding the mandala of the Lord of Speech as well, one should know that the drawing of all the outer lines is the same; however, the specific details shall be explained once more.
One should fashion a circular *sarvatobhadra* for the outer wheel,
taking the base from beneath one cloth and extending the thread from beneath another cloth.
With a beautiful, perfectly circular [compass], one should draw the outer wheel. Grasping the cloth from its base, one should mark it from beneath the cloth of the other side.
One should rotate it seven times without exceeding the measurement of the thread. Having left a space equal to two door-widths in the middle of the central thread.
Without overstepping the sequence of the lines, one should draw seven circles; within the central lines, having left the space between the two doors.
A single thread should be laid out, extending as far as the two corner threads;
that thread serves as the base for the second mandala.
One should draw a single line between the two corner lines; that line is also the base for the second maṇḍala.
It is provided with arches, turrets, and gates;
and in the center of that third mandala is the root [mandala].
It is without archways and possesses door-sockets; it is endowed with doors that are level [with the wall]. Within that, it is the base of the third maṇḍala.
Having abandoned the two doorways, one should likewise drop the cord;
thus, it is adorned with arches, pilasters, and other gate-projections.
Since the two doors have been completely abandoned, the lines should likewise be drawn; it is adorned with archways, doorframes, doors, and door-panels, and so forth.
And within this too, there is likewise a fourth mandala;
just as there is a nine-square grid in the center of the Vajradhātu, so it is here as well.
Furthermore, within that very interior, the fourth maṇḍala is likewise; just as it is within the Vajradhātu, so too here is there a nine-square grid.
Outside the thorn [of the lotus] here, there should be a golden ground four finger-breadths wide;
likewise, a garland of vajras and again a garland of jewels should be fashioned.
Outside the enclosure here, on the golden ground, there shall be four finger-breadths; likewise, one should fashion a vajra garland, and likewise, a jewel garland.
Likewise, there is a row of lotuses and again a row of wheels;
then, by those remaining situated on the outside, twelve finger-breadths of rays [are formed].
The lotus garland is likewise; the wheel garland is likewise again. In the same way for the remaining positions, there are twelve finger-widths of external light rays.

Thus, the laying out of the mandala, which measures sixteen cubits including its retinue and garland of rays, has been explained. Elsewhere, however, it should be understood by following this same principle. || 0 ||

Thus, one should describe the lines of the mandala, which, together with its retinue, measures sixteen cubits and extends to the limit of the light rays; furthermore, other [mandalas] should be understood by following this same procedure.
Just as the wheel of the Āryīya school consists of thirty-two deities,
by that very same sequential application, the wheel purifies the miserable states of existence.

The thirty-two-deity deity [mandala], according to the system of the Noble [Nāgārjuna] and just as in the *Cakrasaṃvara*, is the *Cakrasaṃvara* for purifying the lower realms through the application of the stages of reality (*tattva*).
However, a distinction exists within the *Vajramālā*:
[therein] is a yellow eight-spoked wheel, devoid of vajra-pillars and the like. || 0 ||
As for what should be understood within the *Vajramālā-viśeṣa*: having set aside the *Vajramālā* and so forth, there is a yellow wheel with eight spokes.
Having left a space equal to the door-width inside the central line of the root-sūtra,
three lines should be drawn extending as far as the two corner-lines.

Within the interior of the root lines, having set aside the space between the gates, one should apply three lines between the two diagonal corner lines. Having abandoned one measure (mātrā), one should again draw a single line;
then, having abandoned four measures, a line should likewise be applied.
Having set aside one small part, one should again mark a single line; then, having again set aside four small parts, one should likewise apply the line.
In the center, there are nine squares surrounded by a garland of vajras;
one should know this to be the four-layered maṇḍala of Bhūtaḍāmara. ||o||
In the center is a nine-pointed [vajra]; it should be understood as being like the circular palace of Mañjuvajra. This is the mandala for subduing elemental spirits (*bhūta*).
Now the laying out of the lines for the mandala of Pañcaḍāka is described: having set aside four and a half mātrās on each side of the Brahma-line.
Now, the lines for the maṇḍala of the five ḍākinīs shall be described: from the Brahma-line, at each respective distance, one should omit four and a half units.
Having divided that into twelve parts and set aside two parts on each of the two sides,
leaving out the base, the central axis should be made eight parts long.
One should proceed as follows: there, having set aside two small parts on each of the two sides, one should draw the root lines; [and] within that, one-eighth of the inner part.
The measurement for the door-panels and so forth should be made without the archway (toraṇa),
excluding the *mātrikā* and including four mandalas in the cardinal directions.

According to that measurement, one should construct the doors, door-surrounds, and so forth, but without a pediment (*toraṇa*). Having omitted one part, in all directions, for each of the four maṇḍalas as well—
By this sequential method, the thread should be laid down by the wise;
outside the mandala in the cardinal directions, the ground should be known to be one and a half mātrās.
By means of this sequence of application, the wise should lay out the lines; one should know that in the directions, the outer ground of the maṇḍala occupies two and a half minor units.
In the wheel of Vajraḍāka, within the central maṇḍala,
one thread should be laid out to form a square on all sides.
Furthermore, within the root maṇḍala of the Vajraḍāka-cakra, one should apply a single line; it is perfectly square on all sides.
Furthermore, the matrix sūtra, characterized by a vajra-garland,
has the shape of a half-moon and is beautifully adorned in its center.
Again, from one part, draw the line; it is the mark of the vajra-garland. With a form equal to half a moon, it should be beautifully adorned in the center.
In the circle of Buddha-Ḍāka, it is surrounded by a garland of vajras;
that of Ratna-Ḍāka is encircled on all sides by jewels.
The Buddha-ḍākinī wheel is perfectly circular with a garland of wheels; it is completely and beautifully encircled by the jewels of the Ratna-ḍākinī.
Furthermore, one should cause a [mandala] resembling eight parts of a jewel to be made in its center;
within the wheel of Padmaḍāka, there is the Mātrikā and a garland of lotuses.
It is like the eightfold jewel; one should again place it in the center. Within the maṇḍala of the Padma-Ḍākinī, there is a garland of lotuses upon the minor units (*kalā*).
It should be made in the shape of a four-cornered lotus; in its center, within the wheel of Viśvaḍāka, there is a garland of swords consisting of the mātrikās.
One should construct a square and a lotus shape in its center; furthermore, for the maṇḍala of the Viśvadhāraṇī, there is a garland of swords measuring one small unit.
The wise Vajrācārya should draw a triangle in the center;
the arrangement of the doors and other features should be made according to the measurement of their respective maṇḍalas. ||o||
In its center, a triangle should be made by the wise Vajra Master. According to the dimensions of each respective mandala, the gates and so forth should be carefully determined.
In the mandala of the Six Chakravartins, the lines should be laid out by those who are discerning;
having set aside four *mātrās* on both the right and left sides of Brahmā.
The wise one should bestow the vidyās upon the maṇḍala of the six cakravartins; having omitted four minor units (kalā) to the right and left of Brahmā.
By means of these eight measures, one performs the turning of the mandala;
having made it equal to the twelve limbs, one places two parts on each of the two sides.
Within these eight small parts, one should fully complete the mandala; having made both halves equal, [one should place] two parts on each side.
Having abandoned the doors and so forth, one should again perform [the rite] without a toraṇa,
according to the measurement of the great maṇḍala, having indeed omitted two units of measure.

Having abandoned [the previous measurements], one should construct the doors and so forth; furthermore, there is no pediment (toraṇa). According to the dimensions of the great maṇḍala, one should also abandon two units (kala) [of the total].
A circular line should be drawn for the purpose of measurement using one and a half [units];
then, from that Brahma-line, another circle is likewise [drawn] at an interval of ten units.
For the purpose of measurement, the practitioner should draw a circular line; then, likewise, one should draw [lines] outward again, up to ten minor units (kalā).
Having made five divisions, one should fashion five mandalas;
afterwards, one should erase the circle and the other secondary lines.
Having divided [the space] into five parts, one should likewise construct the five maṇḍalas; thereafter, the circles and the other additional lines should be removed.
Together with the interior, there are six mandalas;
indeed, in the center of these mandalas, there is a space of three mātras for the sake of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Together with the inner [mandala], there are six mandalas; within those very mandalas, there are three small units for the purpose of the navel.
Then, one should draw a circle on the outside; for the sake of the petals, it should be six mātrās [in width].
There should be eight lotuses, each six mātrās [in size], on the outside in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Therefore, for the sake of the petals as well, one should make a circle with six small units; outside, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, there are eight lotuses of six small units each.
Outside of that, there is one square, and again likewise at an interval of one *mātrā*;
the characteristics of the gates and so forth should be known according to the measurement of their respective mandalas. || 0 ||
After that, one circle; from the intermediate small part, again likewise. One should understand the characteristics of the gates and so forth according to the dimensions of their respective maṇḍalas.
Furthermore, other specific types of seven-layered and other maṇḍala-pavilions should be inferred by the wise according to what has been stated and drawn out [in the form of a diagram]. || 0 ||

Furthermore, regarding the specific features of other celestial palaces, such as the mandala of the sevenfold palace, those skilled in measurement should cast the lines following the explanations provided therein.

Furthermore, regarding the mandala taught in the *Śrī Kālacakra*, a dissimilar procedure has been explained for the sake of converting [beings] such as Sūryaratha, which differs from all the rituals taught in other tantras mentioned here.

Therefore, for the practitioner of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), it is the Blessed Lord Śrīvajradhara himself who, through his various forms as the sovereign of all maṇḍalas, has the power to accomplish every intended goal. With firm conviction, one may perform rituals such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) even according to the procedures of other tantras; this accomplishes what is desired without contradiction. Thus, setting aside the elaborate details of the *Kālacakra* system, only the measurement of the maṇḍala lines is described here.
Furthermore, the mere casting of colored powders (*rajaḥpāta*) will be explained later in the section concerning the casting of powders.
