Therefore, practitioners of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) should cultivate firm and superior conviction that the Blessed One, Śrī Vajradhara himself, as the Lord of all mandalas through his manifold bodies, generates and brings forth all desired accomplishments; thus, even the assemblies of other tantras are authorized for consecration and so forth.

Because it is necessary, one accomplishes what is intended. Therefore, having completely set aside the elaborate ritual activities of the *Kālacakra*, only the drawing of the maṇḍala lines will be described here. As for the scattering of colored powders (*rajas*), that too will be explained at the occasion of describing the scattering of colored powders.

In this context, twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) constitute one cubit (hasta) for the preceptor; four cubits form the [side of the] maṇḍala. One should lay down two Brahma-threads measuring eight cubits in length, which is double that [side-length]. Following that, one should likewise lay down two diagonal threads. As for the thread, its thickness should be equal to the measure of a barley grain (yava) for the preceptor. In that mental maṇḍala, the unit (mātrā) to be employed is half a finger-breadth, which is one-sixth of a door-measure.

Here, twenty-four finger-breadths of the master constitute one cubit (*hasta*), and four cubits constitute the mandala. Its width should be twice that, and two *brahma*-lines of eight cubits each must be drawn. Following that, two corner-lines are likewise to be drawn. The thickness of the marking cord is equal to the measure of a grain of barley for the master.
In that regard, one-sixth of the door of the heart mandala is the measure of half a thumb; this shall be designated as a "small unit" (cha chung).
Having fixed the thread at the navel for the purpose of the seal (mudrikā), the Vajra-holder should make it two mātrās in circumference;
then, for the sake of the petals, he should make it four mātrās.
Having fixed the *thig* at the very center, one should make two minor units for the purpose of the navel; then, the Vajra-holder should make a circle with four minor units for the petals.
Then, a continuous thread should be laid out to form a square on all sides; furthermore, at the interval of one matra, another line should be given for the purpose of marking the vajra-garland.
Then, immediately thereafter, the lines are drawn; it is square on all sides. Again, one should provide [the measurements] from the intermediate units; it is marked with vajra-garlands.
Leaving an interval of one *mātrā* between the fourth [line] and the thread reaching up to the two corners,
and again leaving an interval of one *mātrā*, [one draws] the thread for the *vajrāvalī*.

Having set aside four small units (kalā), one should draw the lines reaching the two corners; then, having again discarded the small units in between, one should strike the lines for the vajra-garland.
In the center of this, one should indeed fashion a very beautiful lotus measuring four mātras; on both sides, one should make two pillars, each measuring one mātra.
In the center of this, there is a lotus, most beautiful, measuring four units; furthermore, in both directions, pillars should be made, each measuring one unit.
On the two sides of those [pillars] are two kalaśas, each three mātrās in width according to the layout;
furthermore, the two pillars are one mātrā [in width] and four mātrās in length.
On their faces is a vase three units wide; furthermore, the pillar itself is one unit [in width], and its height is four units.
Then, from the final outer thread, one should cast an external thread,
leaving aside a space of one *muni*, up to the two corner threads.
Subsequently, one should draw the outer boundary line outside of that [inner limit]; having completely discarded one *mātrā*, it lies between the two corner lines.
Outside of that, having set aside four units (mātrās) for the row of deities (devatāpaṭṭī),
and then having set aside another unit, one should cast the root-line (mūlasūtra).
Outside of that, on the divine cloth, one should exclude four *kalās*; then, having excluded the intermediate *kalā*, the root lines should be clearly drawn.
And at the conclusion of the root sūtra is the supreme mandala of the mind;
its doors are one-eighth of the circle, and their width is one-sixth of that.
Reaching the limit of the root lines, it is the center of the heart-maṇḍala; the eighth part of the wheel is the door, and one-sixth of that is a minor unit (kala).
The ritual procedure for the mandala of Kālacakra should be performed by her.
The projections, the pilasters, and the side-walls are to be of the same measurement as the doors.
The conventional designation for this is the mandala of the Kālacakra. The archway is measured according to the dimensions of the door; the same applies to the corners and the sides.
The altar is half of that;
the performance area is half of the altar; the garland should be the measure of the altar; and the jeweled ground is half of that.
Half of that shall be for the pedestal; half of the pedestal shall be for the painting; the lattice shall be equal in measure to the pedestal; the jeweled ground shall be half of that.
The ground for the bakulī and kramaśīrṣa [types] is equal to that of the rajobhū;
its pillar is one and a half mātrās high, adorned crosswise with jewels and other ornaments.

The ground for the *śarbu* and the *iṣṭikā* is equal to the ground for the colors; the pillar is one and a half *caturtha*-parts, and the space between them consists of the seven [jewels] beginning with the precious gem.
It stands seven and a half cubits in length;
and above that, there should be a triple-gated archway.
It stands perfectly at a height of six and one-half cubits; above that, there shall be a triple-tiered pediment.
The height should be three times the measure of the door, which is auspicious.
Therein, the first city is six *mātrās* in measure, and the second is four and a half.
Above that, at a height three times the width of the door, it is beautifully proportioned; there, the first tier is six parts, while the second is four and a half.
The third story is said to be three and a half mātras, while the second story is two mātras;
and above that, the pinnacle (kalaśa) should likewise be two mātras.
The third [section] is said to be three and a half small units (kala); the roof-ridge is described as two small units. The vase situated directly above that shall be two small units.
In that regard, in the first city, the first band should be one *mātrā* [in width] and twenty-four [units] in length; above that, there is another one *mātrā*.
In the first tier, the first cloth-strip is one unit long and twenty-four units wide. Above that, there is another unit;
the *mattavāraṇapaṭṭī* is sixteen units in length, and the place for the worship-deity (*pūjādevatī*) is four units, most beautiful.
The cloth for protecting against delusion is sixteen small units (kala) in length; in its center above that is the very abode of the offering goddesses.
Above that, in the center, the wise Vajrācārya should fashion [the central pillar];
on its two sides, he should fashion two pillars, each one mātrikā in measure.
A fourth part, beautifully adorned, should be made by a wise Vajrācārya; furthermore, on its sides, pillars should be made for each individual unit.
Furthermore, there is the station of the goddess on both sides;
likewise, there are two mother-pillars on both sides in the same manner.
Furthermore, in the two directions of the offering goddesses, it is likewise; and in the directions of the minor pillars, it is exactly the same.
And on both sides, one should place two lions trampled by a lordly elephant;
and above those two lions, one should likewise place their heads.
On both sides, there is a lion with joined tusks; upon the head of that lion, [the wheel] is raised, and likewise again upon their crowns.
The band should be half a mātrā wide and eighteen units in length;
above that should be the band known as the *mattavāraṇa*.
The woolen cloth will be divided into eighteen small pieces; even so, it remains long. Upon that, what has become the woolen cloth is called "the protection against intoxication."
It should be one *mātrā* in width and twelve *mātrās* in length;
above that, there should likewise be a band (*paṭṭī*) three *mātrās* in width and [the same] in length.
The width is one small unit (aṃśuka), and the length is twelve small units. Above that, likewise for the length, there are three small units for the border of the cloth.
In that [area], the four pillars should be constructed with a measurement of three-quarters of a mātrā;
the station of the deities is indeed situated within the intervals between the pillars.
Even with a small portion less than a foot, one should construct four pillars; the dwellings of the goddesses are situated precisely between those pillars.
Furthermore, the mantra-practitioners should perform the three measures and the three locations;
moreover, two *śālabhañjikā* (statues) should be placed on the outer sides of the two pillars.
The mantra practitioner should again perform the three locations endowed with the three small lines; on the outer side of the pillars, one should fashion the goddesses who support the beams.
Furthermore, there should be a transverse band across the two heads measuring half a mātrā;
that same band, well-positioned, should measure fifteen mātrās in length.
Above that, at the crown of the head, there is again a square measuring half a unit; it is perfectly situated with a length of fifteen units.
The *mattavāraṇapaṭṭī*, however, would be one *mātrā*;
above that, it should be eight *mātrās* long; and above that, it should be two *mātrās*.
Above that, for the protection against intoxication, there is one part on the woollen cloth; its length shall be eight parts. Above that, there is a second part.
That [line] likewise should be long; upon it, there should be four pillars, measuring half a mātrā in width and standing two mātrās in length.
Furthermore, its length is suchness; it also has four pillars, possessing a measurement of half a small unit (kalā) in width and two small units in length.
The three positions, each measuring two mātrās, are situated within the pillars;
on the sides of the two outer pillars, there are female statues (śālabhañjikā) as before.
The second small unit of the three positions is also correctly situated between the pillars; on the outer faces of the pillars, as before, are the goddesses who support the beams.
Above that, however, there is a half-mātrā; the beam (paṭṭī) shall be twelve mātrās in length, and above that, it is situated upon the cornice (harmi).
Above that, the lower portion consists of twelve small units; it is long [in that way]. Above that, the roof-ridge is properly situated.
The long [measure] is eight mātrās; above that is situated the vase (kalaśa).
On its left and right sides, one should fashion vajra-banners.
It is eight finger-widths long; above that is the location of the vase. To its right and left, one should place victory banners and flags.
It should be adorned at the tips of all its ledges with bells, mirrors, and chowries,
and especially with banners and other such ornaments.
At the very top of every woolen cloth [canopy], one should likewise arrange eight [ornaments] distinguished by bells, mirrors, fly-whisks, victory banners, and so forth.
Outside the mind-maṇḍala, however, the speech-maṇḍala should be constructed;
one should determine its measurement as being double the size of the [mind-maṇḍala].

Outside the heart maṇḍala, the speech maṇḍala is to be constructed; its dimensions should be carefully determined as being twice the size of the heart [maṇḍala]. In each of the cardinal directions, it measures twelve *mātrikās*, and the walls and so forth of the mind maṇḍala are covered with successive tiers of cornices.
In each of those respective directions, twelve minor parts there are obscured by the walls and other structures of the heart-maṇḍala, as well as by the *śrīvatsas*.
Outside of that, there is one thread again at a distance of seven mātrās;
and with four mātrās, there is again the deity-band (devatā-paṭṭikā).
Outside of that, a single line extends back for seven *aṃśas*; then, by means of four *aṃśas*, there is again the divine cloth (*devavastra*).
And there are four-petaled lotuses in the cardinal directions of that [mandala];
they should be understood, in brief, as being beneath the archway of the mind.
The lotuses of the four small corners transform; those that correspond to them should be understood as being beneath the archways of the heart, in brief.
The elephant-enclosure, the rampart, and so forth of the second city should be carefully drawn within a space of four mātrās.
The cloth for protecting against delusion and so forth should be drawn with great effort from all sides, even on those of the second tier, up to four small units.
With a displacement of half a mātrā between the two pillars,
the deity-band (devatāpaṭṭikā) is positioned outside the cord at an interval of one mātrā.

Between the two pillars as well, one should bend [the cord] by half a small unit (*aṃśuka*). From the line of the divine cloth (*devapaṭṭikā*), in the intermediate spaces outside, [one should place] small units.
The root-line (mūlasūtra) should be laid out up to the two diagonal lines;
there, the drawing of the door-arches (toraṇa) is to be done according to the previously mentioned sequence.
One should carefully draw the central line between the two diagonal lines; there, the gates and the archways should also be drawn according to the previous sequence.
However, with a measurement double that of the mind-maṇḍala,
the supreme body-maṇḍala is outside the base of the speech-maṇḍala.

Furthermore, the measurement of the heart-maṇḍala is by a measure that is double [that]. From the base of the speech-maṇḍala, one should determine the measurement of the supreme external sound-maṇḍala. In each of the cardinal directions, it is twenty-four mātrās.
By means of a measure that is double that, its dimensions are to be precisely measured; in each of the respective directions, there are twenty-four minor units (aṃśuka).
The walls and other parts of the mandala of speech are covered by the gables;
then, having set aside the measure of Rudra, the cord extends from one corner to the other.
The mandala of speech is obscured by the lines and so forth, as well as the arrows and the central staff. Having removed those fierce minor units (*aṃśuka*), the lines run between the two corners.
Having again abandoned the space of one *ravi*, there is likewise a deity-band (*devatāpaṭṭikā*);
on that band, indeed, there are twelve lotuses.
Again, having abandoned the minor suns, the gods are likewise [arranged]; upon that very woolen cloth, there are also twelve lotuses.
Those twelve measures are divided into seven parts each,
situated on the left and right sides of the central portion of the pericarp.
Those are the twelve minor units (*aṃśuka*). Furthermore, from among them, the center of the minor unit is the navel; to its right and left—
Four petals are to be made on its right and left sides;
eight petals are also to be made on its right and left sides.
The petals should be made fourfold, and on its right and left sides, the petals should be made eightfold; those too, on the right and left.
There should be sixteen petals, and that [mandala] should be triple-layered;
furthermore, by means of the triple-layering, there should be twenty-eight petals.
The petals become sixteenfold; that is the third stage. By becoming three stages, the petals become twenty-eight.
The deity-strip should be drawn outside the [inner] thread,
and the root-thread should be given at a distance of one *mātrā*, extending as far as the two corner-threads.
From the line of the divine cloth, one should also provide the root lines on the outside at intervals of one minor unit, extending as far as the corner lines.
The measurement of the doors and arches has been stated previously as it is here;
however, their measure is indeed double that of the extent of the speech-mandala.
The dimensions of the doors and the archways are exactly as previously described here as well; however, the dimension of the speech mandala should be measured by doubling [those proportions].
Half of the circle of water is pervaded by the archway;
outside the archways of the speech-maṇḍala is the body-maṇḍala.
Even half the circumference of the water is pervaded by the archways; from the archways of the speech maṇḍala, [extends] the outer body maṇḍala.
Twelve-mātrā chariots should be constructed in the middle of the gates;
furthermore, a circle of the earth twelve mātrās in extent should be made.
In the center of the gate, one should construct chariots of twelve units; likewise, for the perimeter of the earth, there should be twelve units.
Outside of that is a circle of water measuring twenty-four units;
outside of that again is a circle of fire measuring twenty units.
Beyond that, the circumference of the water is twenty-four *kalā*; therefore, the circumference of the fire is likewise twenty-four *kalā*.
Beyond that, there should be a circle of wind measuring twenty-four units;
outside of that is the circle of space, measuring twelve units.
Outside of that, however, is a garland of rays measuring twenty-four units;
then, on the perimeter of the wind circle, there are twenty-four units, and outside of that, the perimeter of space is twelve units.
At the beginning of the six circles starting with the earth-circle, one should cause a circle to be drawn;
then, by means of the garland of rays, there shall again be seven circles.
First, among the six concentric circles beginning with that [of fire], one should provide a circle; at the end of the garland of light there is also a circle; thus, there come to be seven circles.
The mandala of the Mind-Vajra is supreme, consisting of the three mandalas;
its cord extends from eight cubits up to the circumference of the earth.
This is the mandala of the Vajra Mind, the supreme essence of the three mandalas; its measurement is eight cubits, extending as far as the circumference of the earth.
Thus is one position. || 0 ||
This refers to one side.

However, when the measurement of the door of the mind-maṇḍala here is combined with the measurement of the door of the speech-maṇḍala, and the door is conceived as consisting of eighteen *mātrās*, such that one-sixth of it is designated as a *mātrā*, then by means of that *mātrā*, the number of *mātrās* for the radiance— from the pericarp of the central deity’s lotus to the edge of the circle— must be calculated.

When the measurements of the door of the heart maṇḍala and the door of the speech maṇḍala are combined here and calculated as eighteen minor units (kala), and one-sixth of that is designated as a minor unit, then by means of those minor units, the number of units should be counted from the pericarp of the central lotus up to the edge of the circle of light.

At that time, however, the second position is as follows: the leader of the Mind-Vajra, whose nature is the three mandalas, is the twelve-cubit mandala; the cord is double that, twenty-four cubits, extending from the beginning of the ground-circle. ||o||

At that time, the Lord Vajracitta is the essence of the three maṇḍalas; the maṇḍala [itself] is twelve cubits, and its cord, which is twice that length, is twenty-four cubits, extending as far as the initial perimeter of the earth. This is the second position.

But when the Blessed One Cittavajra is in the place of Vāgvajra, while Vāgvajra is the leader, the placement of the other deities and so forth is as in the first alternative. And when the inner maṇḍala is four cubits, the second is double that, and the third is double that; then the speech maṇḍala consisting of three circles is sixteen cubits, its cord is double that at thirty-two cubits, extending as far as the edge of the ground circle—this is the third alternative.

When the Blessed One, as the Mind-Vajra, abides in the state of the Speech-Vajra, the Speech-Vajra is the principal; the arrangement of other deities and so forth is as in the first case. Furthermore, when there is a central mandala of four cubits and a second [mandala] twice its size, [the arrangement is as follows].

When that [dimension] is doubled, it is the third; at that time, the mandala consisting of three [mandalas] measuring sixteen cubits is the mandala of speech. When that is doubled, the marking cord (sūtra) of thirty-two cubits extends as far as the first perimeter of the earth. This is the third direction.

When, however, the measure of the door of the previously mentioned mind-maṇḍala is combined with the measure of the door of the previously mentioned body-maṇḍala, and a door of thirty units (*mātrā*) is thus conceived, then one-sixth of that is designated as a *mātrā*. At that time, by means of that *mātrā*, the count of *mātrās* should be performed for the lotus pedestal of the central deity (*nāyaka*) and so forth, up to the end of the circle of light rays. Furthermore, the Blessed One Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*) should be placed in the position of Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), while Body-Vajra remains the central deity (*nāyaka*).

The placement of the other deities and so forth is as in the first alternative. At that time, one should visualize the leader Kāyavajra as the mandala consisting of the three spheres, measuring twenty cubits, with a cord twice that length—forty cubits—extending from the edge of the earth-circle; this is the fourth alternative.

When the dimensions of the gate of the previously described mind mandala and the dimensions of the gate of the previously described body mandala are combined and calculated as thirty minor units (*aṃśuka*), and one-sixth of that is designated as a minor unit, then from the center of the principal lotus up to the end of the circle of light, [the distance] consists of minor units.

One should count them, and the Blessed Lord Vajracitta should also be placed in the position of Vajrakāya. Vajrakāya is the principal deity; the arrangement of the other deities and so forth is as in the first section.

At that time, regarding the body-vajra, it refers to the four directions: the twenty-cubit mandala consisting of the three primary mandalas, and its double, the forty-cubit measuring line, which extends as far as the initial perimeter of the earth.

And so, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the root text states "eight cubits," which is explained as "eight cubits" being double the [size of the] mandala. In that regard, in the *Ādibuddha*, one should make the mind-mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*) twelve cubits; its double, twenty-four cubits, is the measuring-line (*sūtra*). Likewise, the speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) is sixteen cubits, and the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*) is twenty cubits—this is the rule. It has been stated [that this is] by way of doubling the measuring-line.

Furthermore, according to the *Vimalaprabhā*, the phrase "a thread eight cubits long" refers to the primary [thread] being eight cubits; it is explained that the [mandala] thread is twice that. Thus, for the *Ādibuddha*, one should make the heart-mandala twelve cubits, and the thread for that, being twice as long, is twenty-four cubits.
Likewise, it is said that the maṇḍala of speech is sixteen cubits and the maṇḍala of body is twenty cubits; this refers to the [actual] measurement, while the marking cord is twice that size.

Furthermore, for the sake of initiation (*sekārtha*), the mere drawing of the womb-maṇḍala (*garbhamaṇḍala*) is permitted. As it has been said: "For the sake of initiation, there is the maṇḍala, which—according to the family (*kula*)—is devoid of the external wheel. || 0 ||

For the purpose of initiation, even a mere central maṇḍala is permitted to be drawn; as it is said: "For the purpose of initiation, the maṇḍala—or by the power of the family—becomes externally inferior to the wheel."

As for the fact that a door measuring one-ninth of the circle is mentioned in the *Trailokyavijaya-tantra* and the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha-tantra*, we have already refuted this by stating that such a measurement is not currently employed by the masters (*ācāryas*). Furthermore, the standard measurement of the maṇḍala has been stated as well-known; however, it is not merely this much. Thus it was said by the Blessed One:

Furthermore, regarding those [mandalas] taught in the *Trailokyavijaya-tantra* as having nine parts for the gates and wheels, and in the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha-tantra* as having ten parts for the gates and wheels—although masters nowadays do not employ such terminology, I have fully established them here. [The mandala...]
The members of the retinue are also to be depicted with their renowned titles, and not merely these alone. Thus, the Blessed One has said:
"The outer mandala of the lords of Jambudvīpa, or of the universal monarchs (cakravartin), should be drawn extending for a full yojana in every direction."
Having observed the minds of those to be trained, there is no fault whatsoever for a wise person to maintain pride even by choice.

Having drawn the entire maṇḍala at will upon the palm of the hand, they accomplish the purpose declared in the scriptures; what need then be said of [drawing it] on the surface of the earth and so forth?

Whether it be a sovereign of Jambudvīpa or a universal monarch (cakravartin), they should draw the outer mandala extending for a full *yojana* in every direction. Having observed with an impartial mind the inclinations of those beings to be trained, there is not the slightest fault in determining the dimensions according to one's own desire; indeed, all mandalas may be made according to one's own wish.
It is said: "Having drawn it upon the palm of the hand, one accomplishes the purpose taught in the treatises; what need is there to mention [drawing it] on the surface of the earth and so forth?"
Or how many mandalas, divided into infinite varieties, could possibly be described or constructed? As the Blessed One said:
"Who is capable of fashioning mandalas according to their true nature?
Through the yoga with one's own tutelary deity, the construction of the mandala is accomplished."

Thus concludes the procedure for laying out the mandala. || 0 ||
This concludes the ritual for casting the lines upon the maṇḍala.
